Your travel planner needs to turn a few traveler preferences into a reliable, itinerary-style answer that a user can trust, and the demo you linked sets a clear bar for how it should feel. I would start by matching that flow in a thin working build rather than a static prototype.

The closest match I have is a marketing copy generator where off-brand outputs fell from 1 in 5 to 1 in 25 after a focused prompt audit and systematic evaluation [ai_ml:case:prompt-audit-copy-tool]. The same discipline applies to itinerary generation: fixed output schemas, test prompts for budget and date constraints, and a scored review set before anything goes live.

I also built a FastAPI service around the OpenAI API for a contract-QA assistant, with token refresh and error retries that lifted answer accuracy from 61 % to 86 % [ai_ml:proposal:012]. I would reuse that pattern for the backend, with a simple Python web front end and a clear way to edit prompts without touching code.

My plan has three steps: first, I review the demo and list its exact features so we agree on scope; second, I deliver a working app with trip input, generated itinerary and a saved result within the first milestone; third, I tune prompts against your test trips and hand over the code with a short run guide.

Which part of the demo matters most to you: the day-by-day itinerary layout, the budget breakdown, or the way preferences are collected?

Your team needs to find where AI fits in your current business processes, choose technologies that suit them, and connect the result to the systems you already run. I would start with a short process review: map the workflows, data sources and integration points, then rank candidate AI use cases by effort and expected payoff.

The closest example is an LLM lead-qualification agent I built for Keystone Realty with LangGraph, PostgreSQL and Twilio. It cut lead response time from 2 days to 3 hours and freed about 6 hours per agent each week [ai_ml:proposal:047]. For a ticket-heavy workflow, I delivered automatic support-ticket routing that handles 72% of tickets without manual triage [ai_ml:proposal:064]. On the evaluation side, I built a test harness for a contract question-answering assistant at Briefwell that raised answer accuracy from 61% to 86% [ai_ml:proposal:056].

My proposed plan has three steps: a discovery phase that recommends technologies and documents the trade-offs, a pilot integrated with your existing systems and tested against real workflows, and a staff walkthrough with written usage notes before handover.

To scope the discovery phase, which of your current processes creates the most manual work today?

You need a prediction tool that uses your fixed set of variables to make horse race outcomes a little more accurate, and that your team can keep running after handover. The closest project I have is a churn uplift model for a telecom, built with gradient boosting on historic usage, billing and interaction records. It cut churn in the targeted cohort by 11% [ai_ml:case:churn-uplift-telco].

For maintainability, I built a production pipeline for a credit-scoring model using Python, MLflow, Docker and GitHub Actions. It moved releases from monthly to weekly and caught two drift incidents early [ai_ml:cv:main]. I would apply the same setup here so your parameters, data loads and model versions are documented and easy to hand over.

My first step would be a short audit: confirm the data fields, agree on a date-based backtest split so we measure lift honestly, and deliver a baseline model with a brief report on what it does and does not improve. From there we can decide whether to extend the variables.

Which race data source and how many years of history will you supply for the backtest?

Getting the right traffic to the right landing page depends on how well your team's models use the data they already have. A consultant who reviews that setup and leaves the team something they can maintain fits this work.

On a recent project I built an NER pipeline that extracted fields from CVs and reached 91% field accuracy on a 500-document validation set, averaging 2.3 seconds per document on a modest cloud instance [ai_ml:case:resume-parser-ner]. I also set up drift monitoring with Evidently and MLflow that caught two drift incidents early in a credit-scoring pipeline [ai_ml:proposal:041]. Measuring results and watching for drift is what I would bring to your KPI work.

My plan is a short first phase. I would review your current data sources, features and evaluation method, then run one knowledge-sharing session on feature engineering and model evaluation with your AI team. We would finish with a ranked list of changes aimed at CTR and conversion, plus the KPIs to track them. I would keep everything in your existing Python and scikit-learn or PyTorch stack so the team can run it without me.

Which metric do you use to judge a landing page's success today, CTR or conversion?
Yes. Which metric defines success for a landing page, CTR or conversion? What data feeds the traffic distribution today, and how often is the model retrained?
I would plan a two-week review and first knowledge-sharing session, followed by a phase for ranked recommendations and KPI setup. The final timeline depends on the data access and scope you confirm.

Your blog needs prompts that produce posts in one consistent voice, follow a fixed structure, and can be updated quickly when the brief changes.

Off-brand wording is the main risk here. In a recent audit of a marketing copy generator, I sampled 200 generated snippets, measured how often off-brand wording appeared, and rewrote the worst prompts with explicit style cues and a short brand checklist. Off-brand outputs dropped from 1 in 5 to 1 in 25 [ai_ml:case:prompt-audit-copy-tool].

On speed and iteration, I reduced first-response time by 40% on a support-ticket routing project through careful prompt tuning [ai_ml:proposal:067]. I would use the same loop here: test each prompt against sample briefs, log failures, and refine before the full batch. I have seven years of experience in prompt engineering and text classification [ai_ml:proposal:083], and I have also proposed an automated blogging tool that connects ChatGPT with WordPress [ai_ml:proposal:083].

My first step would be to take two of your existing blog briefs, write prompts that match the voice you describe, and check the outputs against your blog structure and a short voice checklist. Each prompt would be stored with a version note so later changes are quick to make.

Could you share one published post or a style guide that shows the Rico Brunner tone, along with your blog structure template?

Your team needs a product-level forecast for the next year, converted into raw material quantities, ready before Friday's supplier discussions. The numbers have to hold up across the table from suppliers.

The closest match I have is a daily demand forecast I built for a bakery chain with nine locations. I worked from two years of point-of-sale data, cleaned missing entries and outliers, added calendar features, and produced per-product daily predictions with an ARIMA model tuned by grid search [ai_ml:case:bakery-demand-forecast]. The client's waste fell by 12% across the board [ai_ml:review:003].

For your report, I would start by pulling the last 12 months of raw material purchases and product sales history from Unleashed, then convert the unit forecast into raw material needs using your product recipes. To validate the numbers, I would cross-check the query output against a manual sample extraction and run a checksum comparison between the source and report datasets [ai_ml:proposal:061]. I would send a draft by Wednesday with the assumptions listed, so you can adjust before Friday.

For the move to CIN7 Core, I would document the report logic in clear, reusable steps so it can be rebuilt on the new system.

Which raw material should the first version of the report focus on?
A close recent project is a daily demand forecast for a bakery chain with nine locations. I was responsible for the full workflow: cleaning two years of point-of-sale data, adding calendar features, and building the per-product forecast model with an ARIMA model tuned by grid search [ai_ml:case:bakery-demand-forecast]. The client reported waste down 12% across the board [ai_ml:review:003].
I would cross-check the query output against a manual sample extraction and run a checksum comparison between the source and report datasets [ai_ml:proposal:061]. I would also reconcile total purchase quantities against the Unleashed records and flag any gaps before the numbers go to your suppliers.

Keeping a podcast visible means a steady stream of clips, Reels and up-to-date show pages, and that work can pull time away from making the show. I can take the coordination off your plate with a repeatable process built from your episode text.

The closest example I have is a batch transcription and chaptering pipeline for a podcast network. It turned 400 back-catalogue episodes into transcribed, chaptered text within a week [ai_ml:case:podcast-transcription-pipeline], and the client rated the work 5/5 and kept the system in their editorial workflow [ai_ml:review:014]. My verified experience is in podcast data and AI work rather than day-to-day social media management, so I would start with the content preparation and build the posting routine from there.

For your first two weeks, I would pull chapter markers and transcripts from recent episodes, pick the strongest moments for YouTube clips and Instagram Reels, and draft a posting calendar with captions and website show-note updates for your review before anything goes live.

Which podcast host and website platform do you currently use?

Turning a finished Figma design into a live WordPress site that matches the mockup, works on every screen, and stays easy for your team to edit is the core of this job. I recently turned a Figma mockup into a pixel-accurate landing page in three days [fullstack:case:figma-to-tailwind-landing]. The client said the site 'looks exactly like we imagined' [fullstack:review:003].

Responsiveness came from following the breakpoints in the design and testing on devices from an iPhone SE to a 27-inch monitor, so the call to action stayed visible and clickable at every width [fullstack:case:figma-to-tailwind-landing].

For this project I would build in Elementor with global colors, fonts and reusable sections, so you can edit text, images and layout without breaking the design. I have also moved a magazine off WordPress, which cut page load from 4.1s to 1.6s [fullstack:case:magazine-headless-migration], so I will check performance as the pages go in.

My first step is to review your Figma file, confirm the breakpoints, and build the header and one full section in Elementor for your sign-off before I do the rest of the pages.

Which breakpoints did you design for: desktop, tablet and mobile, or do you also have a separate wide-screen layout?

Your app is not appearing in every country and on every device, and keeping it updated and downloadable is the core of this job. The first thing I would fix is availability, then the update work.

I recently shipped a habit-tracker mobile app to both app stores in six weeks [fullstack:case:habit-tracker-mobile]. I built it with React Native and Expo to keep one codebase, used local SQLite storage so it works offline, and added push notifications through OneSignal [fullstack:case:habit-tracker-mobile]. That experience covers the release, store-submission, and update cycle your app needs.

My proposed first step is to check the Play Console listing, country availability, and device compatibility settings for the current build, then confirm that both download routes work. After that, I would prepare the update, submit it with a short changelog, and agree on a simple monthly maintenance check.

Which countries and device models have reported the app as missing, so I can start with those?

Keeping a YouTube series in one consistent After Effects motion style, edit after edit, is the core problem here, along with a clear price for each video.

I do not have After Effects motion graphics work to show you, so I won't claim it. My verified work is in web development. On one web project, I measured the result, taking a Lighthouse mobile score from 38 to 91 [fullstack:case:core-web-vitals-rescue], by making focused changes instead of a full rewrite. I would apply the same method to your edits: measure against the reference and change only what is needed.

Proposed first step: review the two tutorial references you linked and one finished video from your series, then deliver one test video at a fixed price. Once the style matches, we agree a per-video rate and a turnaround you can count on each month.

Which finished video from your series should I treat as the style reference?
Yes, two questions: do you have a brand kit with fonts, colors and logo files, and how many videos per month should I plan for?

Your Python AI project has grown into tangled code that is slow and hard to change, and you need gains that land without a full rewrite.

The closest past work is a performance rescue for a slow online store. I raised its Lighthouse mobile score from 38 to 91 by deferring non-critical JavaScript and adding caching headers, keeping the changes minimal instead of rewriting the site [fullstack:case:core-web-vitals-rescue]. On the structure side, I refactored legacy services into micro-services, which reduced server costs by 12% [fullstack:cv:main].

My first step would be a short audit: profile the slowest paths, list the redundant modules, and send a ranked change list for your approval before I touch the code. I would ship changes in small, tested pieces so working functionality stays intact.

Which part of the pipeline is slowest today: the model calls, the data retrieval, or the Python logic itself?
I fit best on work that improves existing code without a rewrite. I raised a store's Lighthouse mobile score from 38 to 91 with targeted changes [fullstack:case:core-web-vitals-rescue], and in another project small checkout tweaks cut abandonment by 8% within two weeks [fullstack:case:woocommerce-tweaks]. I have not shown Python or LLM project work in my evidence, so I would confirm that fit in a short first step.
Do you have a test suite or staging environment, and which Python version and deployment target do you use? Which part of the AI pipeline is slowest today, and are there any modules that must not change during cleanup?
For profiling I would start with cProfile and py-spy to find real bottlenecks, and keep your existing framework rather than swap it out. Before refactoring I would add pytest regression tests, then use ruff for linting and consistency. I would confirm the exact tools after reading the code, since the right choice depends on where the time is actually spent.

Your legal team needs admin work that stays accurate while file volumes and deadlines grow. I have not worked as a legal assistant, so I will be direct about where my evidence comes from. My closest match is an internal CRM that replaced spreadsheets for an estate agency: 35 agents moved off spreadsheets in 8 weeks [fullstack:case:keystone-crm], and automated pulls kept listings current without manual entry [fullstack:case:keystone-crm]. I also built an online booking portal for a clinic network, where 40% of appointments moved online within six months and no-shows dropped by 18% [fullstack:case:patient-booking-portal].

For the scheduling, file and drafting side, I would start with a short plan: in week one, review your current file structure and appointment flow, then draft a checklist for correspondence and document review that your team approves before I take on wider tasks. I am available from Monday and expect about a week for a first pass, depending on scope [fullstack:proposal:111].

Which file or scheduling task currently causes the most delays for your team?
About a week, depending on scope, for a first pass on scheduling and file setup [fullstack:proposal:111].
Available from Monday [fullstack:proposal:111].

Your project needs a reliable way to judge whether MPC actually improves conversion efficiency and grid stability over PID in grid-connected smart hybrid inverters, using data that comes from papers, field logs and simulations. The closest work I have done is a research dataset cleanup for a university team preparing a peer-reviewed submission, where the cleaned data passed the journal's reproducibility check [data_analyst:case:research-dataset-cleanup] and the client confirmed it saved weeks of back-and-forth with reviewers [data_analyst:review:011]. That work covered the same preprocessing discipline your study needs: consistent variable naming, auditable steps, and checks that the output can be reproduced.

For the statistical side, I ran a checkout redesign experiment analysis where the raw numbers were noisy and a misleading result could have driven a bad launch. Careful experiment design and statistics confirmed a +3.1% conversion lift and avoided a false-positive launch [data_analyst:case:checkout-ab-test]. The same approach applies to comparing MPC and PID runs across varied operating conditions and testing whether observed differences hold up.

My proposed first step is a two-week phase: build a source register from the literature and field data, define a common data schema that both simulation and field records map to, and deliver a short report on data quality and the first MPC-versus-PID comparison. I will share a progress note at the end of each week so the team can see where the analysis stands.

Which simulation or field datasets will you provide first, and in what format?
Estimated timeline: about 3 weeks within your 1 to 3 month window. Week 1 covers the literature review and source register. Week 2 covers data collection and preprocessing with a data quality report. Week 3 covers the MPC versus PID statistical comparison and a draft of findings. Revisions and final recommendations can follow after your feedback. This estimate assumes timely access to the datasets.
Yes: (1) Which simulation models and parameter ranges define the MPC and PID baselines? (2) What grid-stability and efficiency metrics are the priority for policy recommendations? (3) What is the expected format and access method for field data, and are there data-sharing restrictions? (4) Who on the team will review the statistical methods before the final write-up?
My closest comparable work is a research dataset cleanup for a university team preparing a peer-reviewed submission [data_analyst:case:research-dataset-cleanup]. I was responsible for consolidating inconsistent CSV files, standardizing variable names, and documenting every transformation so the result passed the journal's reproducibility check [data_analyst:case:research-dataset-cleanup]. The client confirmed the work saved weeks of reviewer back-and-forth [data_analyst:review:011]. I also ran a checkout redesign experiment analysis that used statistical testing to confirm a +3.1% conversion lift and prevent a false-positive launch [data_analyst:case:checkout-ab-test]. My role in both was end-to-end: data preparation, statistical analysis, and clear written findings. I have not worked on inverter control specifically, so I would rely on your team for domain-specific MPC and PID modelling assumptions.

Your three folders of about 20 workbooks each all fail with the same "corrupted data" error when Power Query connects, so you need a fix that works across the whole set and a process you can reuse on future files.

I automate recurring spreadsheet work. For an accountancy firm I built a hub workbook that reshaped ledger exports into client templates, saving 30 staff hours a month and cutting errors in client packs to near zero [data_analyst:case:accountancy-excel-automation]. I also cut a BI team's weekly reporting from two days of spreadsheets to an automated dashboard used by 120 regular users [data_analyst:cv:main].

I have also taught technical skills live. I tutored a career changer in weekly two-hour sessions until they passed two technical interviews [data_analyst:case:sql-tutoring], so I know how to pace a session so each step is clear.

My plan: first, we run a 15-minute check on one failing workbook and one from each folder to find where the error starts. Then the 60-minute Teams or Zoom session covers the fix, the query steps for new columns and averages, and a short written checklist you can apply to future workbooks.

Which of the three folders has the most files showing the error, so I can start there?

The closest project I have is a churn uplift model for a telecom client, where the model targeted retention offers to the subscribers most likely to respond. Churn in the targeted cohort fell 11% while offer spend dropped 30% [ai_ml:case:churn-uplift-telco].

I would start by mapping each variable you define to a tested feature, then build a baseline gradient-boosted model with a holdout set, so we can see whether any gain is real before adding complexity. For the production side, I have built a credit-scoring pipeline with MLflow, Docker and Evidently monitoring, where two drift incidents were caught early [ai_ml:cv:main]. Each model input and parameter would be documented so you can audit how the tool reaches its output.

The first step would be a short plan: a data review, a variable map, and a backtest report on past races. Which data source covers past race results, and how far back does it go?

Your team needs a way to tell which landing page traffic will convert and click through, without adding heavy process to your current models. I would start by reviewing how you currently build features and evaluate models, then turn that into a short, practical plan your team can run. In a recent telecom project, a targeted uplift model cut churn in the targeted cohort by 11% and reduced retention spend by 30% [ai_ml:case:churn-uplift-telco]. The same approach of predicting who will respond, rather than who is in a segment, fits landing page distribution. On the recommendation side, a cold-start system for a reading app raised day-one click-through by 9% using sparse metadata and monthly updates, which suggests a lightweight path for your new pages [ai_ml:case:cold-start-recommender]. For knowledge transfer, I have mentored junior analysts on feature engineering and model evaluation and built monitoring dashboards that cut model-to-production latency from weeks to days [ai_ml:cv:main]. My proposed first step is a two-week audit of your data, features and validation metrics, followed by one workshop for your team and a draft KPI set for CTR and conversion. Which current metric do you trust most today for judging a landing page's performance?
Yes, I have a few questions before starting: which data sources feed your current landing page model, how often are pages and traffic sources refreshed, and which CTR and conversion definitions does your team use today? Knowing your current validation approach would also help me focus the initial review [ai_ml:cv:main].
A realistic estimate is about four to six weeks: two weeks for the data and modelling review, one to two weeks for knowledge-transfer sessions and a workshop, and one to two weeks for KPI setup and handover. This mirrors the phased approach used in a prior churn uplift engagement, where the model was launched and measured within a defined window [ai_ml:case:churn-uplift-telco].

Your blog prompts need to hold your brand voice and structure across every post, without heavy editing afterward. I recently faced this exact problem with a marketing copy generator that kept producing off-brand text. I collected 200 generated snippets, measured the off-brand rate, and rewrote the worst prompts with explicit style cues and a short brand checklist, which cut off-brand outputs from 1 in 5 to 1 in 25 [ai_ml:case:prompt-audit-copy-tool].

I also have experience improving prompts under delivery pressure. On a support-ticket routing project, careful prompt tuning reduced first-response time by 40% [ai_ml:proposal:067]. In another project, I used LangGraph and tool-calling in Python to cut lead-qualification time from 2 days to 3 hours [ai_ml:proposal:036].

My plan: in week one, I review your blog structure, brand samples and keyword targets, then build a prompt template set with SEO slots for keywords and headings. In week two, I test each prompt on three sample briefs, log off-brand and structure errors, and tune until the drafts need minimal edits. After launch, I keep a change log so prompts can be updated as your requirements change. Any German output will be checked by a native German reviewer before you publish.

Which two published posts best represent the brand voice you want me to match?

Your team needs a trustworthy demand forecast and raw material requirement figure before Friday's supplier discussions, and that figure has to hold up under scrutiny. I have built forecasting work that clients act on: a daily demand forecast for a bakery chain cut waste by 12% across nine shops [ai_ml:case:bakery-demand-forecast] and the client credited it with smoother planning [ai_ml:review:003]. That project required the same discipline your report needs, turning forecasts into specific operational decisions.

I would start by pulling the last 12 months of purchase data for the timber line and confirming unit definitions against Unleashed, then build a forecast of next-year units by product and convert it into raw material quantities with clear assumptions. I would deliver a draft by Wednesday with a short sheet showing inputs, formulas, and sensitivity ranges so you can adjust before Friday. I also have experience building reporting pipelines that process structured records reliably [ai_ml:case:invoice-field-extraction], which will help when you move from Unleashed to CIN7 Core and need repeatable reports.

Would it be possible to share a sample of the purchase history export and the current product bill of materials so I can confirm the raw material mapping before I start?
A close match is a daily demand forecast I built for a bakery chain. I developed time-series models that drove a bake-list plan across nine shops, and waste fell 12% over a three-month pilot [ai_ml:case:bakery-demand-forecast]. My role was end to end: data preparation, model build, and translating the output into daily decisions the client's staff could use [ai_ml:review:003]. The same approach applies here: forecast units first, then convert to raw material need.
I would validate in three ways. First, I would reconcile totals in the report back to the Unleashed purchase and sales exports, checking that quantities and periods match. Second, I would cross-check the SQL or formula logic against a manually calculated sample of products to catch errors in the raw material conversion. Third, I would run a checksum-style comparison between source and report datasets so any change in the data is visible before the report goes to suppliers [ai_ml:proposal:061].

Your podcast needs listeners to find each episode and clip across your website, YouTube and Instagram, and that depends on the episode content being easy to search and share.

The closest project I have is a batch transcription and chaptering pipeline for a podcast network with about 400 back-catalogue episodes. We delivered all 400 transcribed and chaptered within a week [ai_ml:case:podcast-transcription-pipeline]. The client said the system is now part of their editorial workflow [ai_ml:review:014].

For your team, the same approach means episode text and chapter markers can feed website pages, show notes and captions for YouTube clips and Reels. I would keep the first step focused on those podcast assets rather than promising results I have not measured for social accounts.

First step: I would review your recent episodes and your current Instagram and YouTube posting schedule, then send a short plan covering which assets to reuse and how often to post. Ongoing part-time coordination would follow once you approve that plan.

Which channel brings in the most new listeners for you today?

I have also built automated login and permission tests that run on every pull request, designed to catch regressions before they reach production.

For your project, I would start with a short audit of the current Cypress specs and CircleCI run times, then fix the slowest and flakiest tests first. After that, I would add new tests for the CRM areas that break most often.

Which parts of the CRM break most often, and how long does the full Cypress run take on CircleCI today?

Do you want the header and footer built with Elementor's theme builder, or kept as regular page sections?

The closest project I have is a habit-tracker mobile app MVP that shipped to both app stores in 6 weeks, with a 4.8-star rating in its first week of download [fullstack:case:habit-tracker-mobile]. Getting a listing live and visible in the stores is directly relevant to your problem.

The closest work I can show is a logo refresh for a neighbourhood bakery, where I digitized a hand-drawn mark in Adobe Illustrator and delivered colour and monochrome versions ready for the sign maker and box printer [fullstack:case:bakery-logo-refresh]. That project needed one clean visual system that holds up across many uses, which is what your series needs.

I should be direct about the gap: I have not yet delivered a motion-graphics project in After Effects, so I would not quote a per-video price until I have reviewed the tutorials and one of your existing videos.

Which tutorial timestamp shows the exact motion you want, so I can start the test with that reference?
Before starting, I would like to know which tutorial timestamp shows the exact motion you want, and how many videos per month you expect so I can set a clear per-video price.

Your Python AI project needs tangled code cleaned up and sped up without a full rewrite, so the parts that already work keep working. My closest match is a performance rescue for a slow online store, where I started by auditing the network waterfall to find the biggest bottlenecks and removed the heaviest dependency. The mobile Lighthouse score went from 38 to 91 [fullstack:case:core-web-vitals-rescue].

I have also written Python background workers for an estate agency CRM that fetched new property data and calculated lead freshness [fullstack:case:keystone-crm]. That is the kind of Python service work your codebase needs.

My plan is incremental. First, I would profile the current code to rank the bottlenecks and share a short written list of proposed changes before editing anything. Then I would refactor one module at a time, check outputs against the current behavior after each step, and document every change so your team can review it.

Which part of the pipeline is the slowest today, and is there a test suite or sample inputs I can use to confirm behavior stays the same after each change?
I have made a slow production site much faster by auditing where time was going and removing the heaviest dependency, which took the mobile Lighthouse score from 38 to 91 [fullstack:case:core-web-vitals-rescue]. I have also written Python background workers for a CRM that fetch data and calculate lead freshness [fullstack:case:keystone-crm]. My evidence does not include LLM or RAG projects, so I am not claiming that experience.

I would refactor the code around them and keep the existing LLM and retrieval calls as they are unless profiling shows they are the bottleneck. Your legal team needs accurate records, current files, and documents that go out without errors, and it needs them handled by someone who can keep up with deadlines.

The closest project I have is an internal CRM that replaced spreadsheets for an estate agency. All 35 agents moved off the old system within eight weeks, and automated pulls kept listings current without manual entry [fullstack:case:keystone-crm]. On a billing project, the finance team stopped reconciling payments by hand once the system took over that work [fullstack:case:tallyhub-billing]. Across my career I have also consistently met tight launch deadlines on client work [fullstack:cv:main].

I am a software developer, not a legal professional, so I am not claiming legal experience. What I bring is careful handling of records, structured data, and deadlines.

My first step would be a paid sample: about 20 data entries and one drafted letter from your templates. That gives you a clear view of my accuracy and pace before we agree on a weekly plan.

Which task would you like me to start with: scheduling, file maintenance, or drafting?
I cannot give a firm timeline until I see the volume and format of the first batch of documents. I would start with a sample of about 20 data entries to measure my pace and error rate, then send you a specific estimate.
I cannot confirm my exact weekly hours for the next two weeks from my profile alone. Once you share the expected workload, I will confirm the hours I can commit to and whether I can begin on the sample batch.

Your project needs MPC and PID results compared on grid efficiency, backed by data you can trace. Before any control comparison can be trusted, the simulation and field data must be accurate and complete. I have done this kind of preparation before: I cleaned a university research team's raw experimental CSV files so they passed a peer-reviewed journal's reproducibility check [data_analyst:case:research-dataset-cleanup], and the client noted it saved weeks of back-and-forth with reviewers [data_analyst:review:011]. I also run statistical analysis on experiments; in a checkout redesign test I confirmed a +3.1% conversion uplift after three weeks and avoided a false-positive launch [data_analyst:case:checkout-ab-test].

My plan: first, collect the papers, technical reports, and simulation outputs into one dataset with a data dictionary. Second, validate and preprocess it in Python. Third, run the MPC versus PID comparison with confidence intervals and share draft findings at the midpoint for your review. I have not worked on inverter control hardware or MPC design myself, so I will rely on your team's domain notes for the control-theory interpretation.

Which simulation and field datasets already exist, and in what format?
The post lists 1 to 3 months. My plan is about two weeks for data collection and preprocessing, two to three weeks for the MPC versus PID analysis, and one week for the written recommendations. The schedule can shorten or lengthen depending on how quickly the datasets are shared.
Which simulation settings, grid parameters, and data sources do you already have? Who on your team will check the control-theory interpretation? Is the final deliverable a written report, an analysis notebook, or both?
The closest project was cleaning a university research team's raw experimental data in CSV files so it passed a peer-reviewed journal's reproducibility check [data_analyst:case:research-dataset-cleanup]. I handled the data preparation and validation end to end, and the client rated the work 5/5 [data_analyst:review:011]. That project was not in power electronics, so MPC and inverter-specific modelling would be new to me, and I would rely on your team for that domain knowledge.
